name: 178. Routing rules: scope precedence, lifecycle, chains, conditions and fallbacks (routing-rule-behaviour)
description:
Wire-level pins for routing rules beyond a single global rule. Every rule is gated on a run-scoped header, every target is a run-scoped OpenAI-backed custom provider, and the provider in routing_info names which rule applied.

Rows: (1) a virtual key in a team under a customer gets its own scope's rule over the team's, the customer's and the global one, and deleting rules one by one hands routing down that chain; (2) disabling, re-enabling and editing a rule each take effect on the next request; (3) a chain rule's rewrite is matched by a second rule, and with chaining off the rewrite to a model that does not exist stands (404); (4) conditions read request_type and the URL query parameters, so a streamed request (chat_completion_stream) or one without the parameter falls through; (5) conditions read the virtual key the request was made with; (6) a rule's fallbacks replace the caller's: its own fallback serves, and with that fallback dead the caller's live one is not tried; a rule whose fallbacks are cleared keeps the caller's; (7) a caller's key pin (x-bf-api-key-id) is tried on the first attempt only, on the provider the request starts on: with a rule targeting another provider, that attempt fails key selection and the rule's fallback serves without the pin, whether or not the caller named the provider; with virtual key weights instead of a rule, a request load balancing starts on the key's provider is served on the pinned key, and one it starts elsewhere is served by the key's provider as a fallback, without the pin. (8) the precedence ladder in one bed: a bare model with a virtual key goes where its weights send it and governance attaches the other weighted provider, a rule sends it past the weights, without a key the catalog picks the first provider by name, a caller that names a provider gets it, and a rule rewrites even that; each request's log names only the engine that decided; a rule target the key does not allow is refused and the rule fallback serves, or the caller gets 403 without one; (9) a rule target beats the virtual key weights, with the trail naming the rule and governance skipping load balancing, and a matched rule gets no fallbacks from governance, so a dead target's error reaches the caller; (10) a provider-only target keeps the caller's model; a model-only target leaves the provider to the virtual key weights, which split across both providers and attach the other as a fallback on the rule's model; with one weighted provider governance picks it for the rule's model and attaches no fallback; (11) a target pinned to a refused key hands over to the fallback's pinned key, a provider-only rule fallback takes the caller's model, and a fallback whose provider was deleted is dropped, so the next one serves as fallback 1; (12) a target pinned to a key that does not serve the model, or that the virtual key's key_ids exclude, fails key selection: the rule fallback serves and becomes the session's route, and without one the caller gets 400; a caller pin outside the key_ids gets 400 too; (13) the last rule of a chain decides the key pin and fallbacks as well as the target, and the trail lists the chain rule as continuing; (14) a rule rewrites a request that named its provider and keeps the requested provider; such a request binds the session's key but not its route, so each turn starts at the named provider; (15) a pinned target keeps its key through a session, a pin added mid-session wins until it is removed and the session's key then returns, and two targets on one provider pinned to different keys split between them; (16) a fallback pinned to a disabled key cannot serve, so the primary's error is returned with the primary's headers, and a caller's direct key takes the place of the rule's pin on the first provider only: a refused one leaves the fallback to serve on its own pin without binding the session, and a working one (the runner's openaiKey) serves on the target and binds the session's route but no key; (17) the key selector ladder on one provider: direct key, rule pin, caller key id, caller key name, session binding, weights, with no pinned request rebinding the session, and a virtual key's key_ids refusing a pin outside them; (18) reordered rule fallbacks reach unbound requests while a bound session keeps its fallback; of two matching rules in one scope the lower priority wins, a duplicate priority is refused with 409, and a priority change takes effect on the next request. (19) a rule that rewrites a bare model to another provider's model serves it there on one attempt, reports the requested and served models, and binds the session's route under the requested model to the rewritten route; (20) two weighted rule targets without fallbacks split 2012 requests 70/30 within a 5.1-standard-deviation band and pass chi-square at p > 1e-6, every request a primary on one of them; (21) a header rule and a request-type rule coexist: each request matches only its own, a request neither matches goes to the catalog, and the trail names each rule that did not match with the variables it read; (22) weighted targets without fallbacks re-roll every turn of a session, which drops its binding on every turn the roll moves and rebinds to what served; (23) weighted targets with fallbacks hold a session on its first provider, moved first whenever the roll proposes the other; (24) a rule edited under a bound session keeps the provider and its key while the chain offers them, drops a key that stops serving the model, and drops the provider once the chain leaves it out; (25) a provider deleted and added back under the same name keeps a binding no turn refused, while a turn made without it moves the session for good; (26) one hundred identical turns under a rule, a virtual key and a session take the same provider and key with the same trail from turn 2. Each row deletes what it made. Run with FEATURE="routing-rule-behaviour".
